name: Climate and the Economy
title: Climate and the Economy
answer: Climate and the Economy covers how physical climate hazards and the transition to lower emissions show up in macroeconomic aggregates: output, productivity, employment, inflation, trade, public finances and financial stability. It sits inside macroeconomic econometrics, so the unit of interest is usually a country, sector or region observed over decades rather than a single firm or household. The work spans damage estimation, transition scenario design, and measurement of the effects of policies such as carbon pricing or subsidy reform. It also covers the feedback loop in which climate shocks change prices and investment, which in turn changes emissions.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Climate and the Economy covers how physical climate hazards and the transition to lower emissions show up in macroeconomic aggregates: output, productivity, employment, inflation, trade, public finances and financial stability. It sits inside macroeconomic econometrics, so the unit of interest is usually a country, sector or region observed over decades rather than a single firm or household. The work spans damage estimation, transition scenario design, and measurement of the effects of policies such as carbon pricing or subsidy reform. It also covers the feedback loop in which climate shocks change prices and investment, which in turn changes emissions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on long panel datasets that combine national accounts, input-output tables, energy balances, price indices and trade statistics with gridded climate data from satellites, weather stations and reanalysis products. Firm-level emissions and disclosure records are increasingly joined to these panels, along with asset-level data on plants, power generation and land use. Computation is modest by machine learning standards: regression and simulation code in R, Python or Stata, plus integrated assessment models and general equilibrium solvers that can take hours to converge. Storage and versioning matter more than raw compute, because a result is only as good as the vintage of the data behind it.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Estimation typically starts with panel regressions that include country and time fixed effects, so a temperature or precipitation anomaly is identified against a within-unit baseline rather than a cross-sectional difference. Dynamic responses are traced with local projections or structural vector autoregressions, and longer-run policy questions are handled in dynamic stochastic general equilibrium models with an energy or climate block. Scenario analysis is central: transition pathways are imposed as assumptions about carbon prices, technology costs and policy stringency, then run through the model to produce ranges rather than point forecasts. Machine learning appears mainly in nowcasting, downscaling and the construction of high-frequency indicators, and uncertainty is reported through confidence bands, ensembles or sensitivity grids.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is the hard part, because climate and economic series come from different agencies with different revision cycles, spatial resolutions and licences. Disclosure frameworks such as the TCFD recommendations and the ISSB standards shape what firm-level data exists, and those data are often self-reported and inconsistently scoped across emissions categories. Reproducibility requires documented code, frozen data vintages and clear statements about which scenario assumptions drive a result. Scenario output is conventionally labelled as conditional on its assumptions rather than presented as a forecast, and the field treats model disagreement as information rather than noise.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward finer spatial and sectoral resolution, so a heat wave or a flood can be mapped to the plants, workers and supply chains it touches. Central banks and finance ministries are extending climate stress tests and scenario exercises, which pushes the field toward harmonised transition pathways and comparable physical risk metrics. Better firm-level disclosure and satellite measurement should reduce reliance on country averages, though gaps in low-income economies are likely to persist. Expect more real-time indicators, more explicit treatment of uncertainty, and closer integration between econometric estimates and the process-based climate models that supply the shocks.
